text: Whoever has the ball controls the game, so a team should always want more possession than its opponent.
Dominating a game means creating more danger, even with less of the ball.
Against a weaker side that sits back, my team should keep the ball and move it around until a gap opens.
With fast forwards in the squad, I let the opponent have the ball so there is space behind their defense.
Having the ball is also a way of defending, because while we have it the opponent can't attack.
If the striker is free behind the defense, the long ball is the right pass.
If the opponent presses high, we should still play out from the back with short passes, even with the risk near our own box.
Every sideways or backward pass is a wasted chance to attack.
I prefer a defensive midfielder who never loses the ball to one who risks line-breaking passes.
When the team wins the ball back, it has to get a shot away within three or four touches.
Each player should hold his zone of the pitch, so the team keeps its shape even when attacking.
The best attacks come from players close together, combining in tight spaces like in a rondo.
If the winger leaves the touchline to come inside for the ball, he is getting his job wrong.
The striker should drop out of the box to combine with the midfielders, not just wait for the ball.
A good team is recognized by well-defined positions, where everyone knows exactly where to be in each phase of play.
Games are won by wingers beating the full-back one-on-one and crossing.
The shortest route to goal is through the middle, and that is where a team should put its best players.
Against a defense packed in the middle, the best option is to stretch the pitch and get the ball into the box from the flanks.
I'd rather pick an extra central midfielder than keep two wingers hugging the touchline.
A team without wide wingers becomes predictable and easy to defend against.
When the team loses the ball, it has to try to win it back immediately, near the opponent's box.
Defending near your own box, with the lines close together, is the safest way not to concede.
The forwards are the first defenders and should press the opposing center-backs from the very first pass.
Against an opponent who plays out well from the back, I'd rather drop off and wait than press their build-up.
Winning the ball in the opponent's half is worth more than any rehearsed move.
Defenders should protect spaces, not chase an opponent around the pitch.
If the opponent has a star player, I put someone on him to mark him closely for the whole game.
With man-marking everyone knows who their opponent is, and it's clear who was at fault for a goal.
When defending a corner, I'd rather each player protect an area than each mark an opponent.
Zonal marking gives the opponent too much freedom to think.
When arriving at a new club, the coach imposes his idea and the players who adapt to it get to play.
Studying the opponent's weaknesses matters more than drilling your own game model.
Level at half-time, I adjust details but keep the plan, because the goal will come.
Against a far stronger team, the right thing is to give up your own idea and play to neutralize them.
A team should play its own way, whoever the opponent is.
A team that plays beautifully and loses is still remembered, and that matters.
Away from home against a strong team, a draw is already a great result.
Winning a final in the last minutes, I bring on an extra center-back and shut the game down.
How the team won matters more than the score.
Fans go to the stadium to see their team win, not to watch a show.
A good system turns ordinary players into great ones.
If the winger has lost his first three dribbles, he should keep trying, because he is the one who decides the game.
If the star doesn't track back, he goes to the bench, because here everyone does their job.
The coach should give the star freedom instead of tying him to a tactical role.
I'd rather have eleven average players who know the plan by heart than eleven stars improvising.
I'd rather pick a slow player with great technique than a fast one who can't control the ball.
Without physical intensity, you can't compete in today's football.
There is still room for the classic number 10, even if he doesn't run that much.
When signing a defensive midfielder, strength and stamina count for more than passing quality.
Big games are decided by fifty-fifty challenges and aerial duels.
A club should be built with players from its own academy.
Fighting for the title, I'd rather start a seasoned veteran than a promising youngster.
If the academy kid and the expensive signing are at the same level, the kid plays.
Titles are won with experienced players, and young players need time to mature.
Developing players is as important for a club as winning titles.
The coach is the boss, and the stars follow the same rules as everyone else.
A happy, united group performs better than a dressing room run with an iron fist.
If the best player disagrees with the line-up, the coach should listen to him before deciding.
A player who turns up late for training misses the next game, whoever he is.
A coach's role is more about looking after people than giving orders.
